transcription.text: Hi, welcome to the EEVblog, an electronics engineering video blog of interest to anyone
involved in electronics design. I'm your host, Dave Jones. Well, there it is, April 1st, 2011.
If you saw my last blog, you'll know that I couldn't resist myself. I did a triple five
timer scam, and yes, it was complete bullshit, of course. There is no secret hidden easter egg
in the triple five timer. Sorry, Hans, I couldn't resist including you to help sell the story.
And, uh, if you're wondering how I did it, it's pretty simple. Let me show you. What, uh, what
you see here is real, but what you didn't see off camera is there's a second oscillator.
InfiniiVision scope. Let's take a closer look. Okay, here it is. I've got, I'm using the waveform
generator output. I'm generating a sine wave at, you guessed it, 55.5 hertz at about half a volt.
It's AC coupled. It goes into a little secret hidden switch here, which I was using to, uh, turn
the signal off and on off camera that you didn't see. Now, of course, there's nothing connected
to pin 5 here, of course, which is the modulation you can use for modulation input on the triple
five timer. Frequency modulation. Now, uh, but what you didn't see are these wires running under
the ESD mat. There they go. And they pop up through a hole in the ESD mat at the bottom.
And on the bottom here, I just drilled a hole through the breadboard. There it is. And I soldered
that, uh, that oscillator signal directly onto pin 5, the little strip inside on the bottom of
the breadboard for pin 5. So that's how I was able to do it off camera. I just flicked that switch
whenever I wanted to cue the modulation. And that's it. Pretty darn simple. I hope you enjoyed it
and catch you next time. Sorry Hans. And if you've never actually seen under a breadboard before,
I highly recommend you just unscrew the, uh, screws on the bottom and lift it out. And lo and behold,
there are the individual strips. And you can see how there's the, uh, break up here in these power
strips up there. And there's the individual, uh, strips. And you can actually just pop these out
if you want. Um, and you can just solder directly on there, which is what I did. And the baseboard
just holds those in. In fact, you can buy these that don't have the baseboard and they'll just
have, like, a paper backing on them. One of the first breadboards I ever got when I was a kid
actually just had, it was a Radio Shack Tandy one, and it just had paper on the back like that. So
that's all that holds them in. And you can see exactly what the strips are like. Have a play
around with it. See ya!
